title: Forced Event Liquidity
market_niche: Corporate-action, index-change, and event-driven situations where some participants must transact.
phenomenon: Forced or mandate-driven trades may create temporary pressure that later mean-reverts.
counterparty_or_forced_actor: Index funds, benchmark-constrained managers, corporate-action processors, tax-motivated sellers, and funds facing mandate or liquidity constraints.
why_edge_might_exist: Some participants may transact for mandate, benchmark, tax, or operational reasons rather than expected return.
why_large_funds_might_ignore_it: Each event may be too small, too operationally messy, too data-cleaning-heavy, or too liquidity-constrained for large capital.

institutional_constraint_evidence.expected_daily_dollar_volume: unknown until event universe is sourced

expected_capacity: Likely low to moderate and highly dependent on event type and liquidity.
expected_holding_period: Days to months depending on the event.
persistence_mechanism: Mandates and operational constraints can recur even after the broad pattern is known.
crowding_risk: Medium to high in obvious events; lower in fragmented or annoying-to-clean niches.
edge_decay_trigger: The opportunity should decay if event liquidity improves, indexes change rules, or event effects vanish after spread assumptions.
observable_prediction: Event cohorts with forced-flow pressure should show measurable post-event drift or reversal after realistic trading frictions.
falsification_tests: Reject if the effect disappears after realistic spread and liquidity assumptions.
Reject if the data source cannot distinguish real events from survivorship-biased samples.
Keep as untested until event data quality is auditable.
suggested_validation: Do not backtest until event data provenance is documented.
Analyze cohorts by event type and liquidity bucket.
references: Practitioner literature on index reconstitution and event-driven forced flows
Academic literature on price pressure around index changes
